questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] operating a workflow engine: retries by error class, stuck runs (relay, docs/adr/0009-durable-execution.md). Requirements: about 200,000 runs a day across 40 workers; each run is 3-6 steps calling third-party vendors (email and sheets honour an Idempotency-Key, the chat vendor offers none); vendors return 503s and 429s and sometimes simply hang; you deploy ten times a day; after a vendor outage you must be able to recover 10,000 failed runs without double-sending anything. Write your design before you look: what a step records and when, which failures retry and who decides, what happens to a step that never returns, how a deploy mid-run behaves, and how recovery replays work. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Each StepRun is a durable state machine whose checkpoint commits before the run advances; on resume a succeeded step rehydrates its stored output instead of running its side effect again.
keyPoints.quote: Never take step N+1's word for step N.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Every step derives one idempotency key that stays the same across every retry and resume and is sent with the call, so the vendor that performed the effect can refuse a repeat even when our own checkpoint never got written.
keyPoints.quote: even when our checkpoint is missing, the key already reached the arbiter of truth

keyPoints.text: [w3] Retry is decided by the error's class from a closed taxonomy in one engine-owned table: transient classes earn a delayed retry under a hard attempt cap, deterministic ones never retry, and adding a vendor adds no retry code.

[w3] A hung socket raises no error, so no retry class ever fires: each active step needs a duration budget (expected time x grace factor) and a heartbeat to tell slow from dead, and the timeout must lead to a parked, replayable state rather than a verdict.
[w2] Contain the blast radius per connector: a breaker that trips on a degraded connector holds only that connector's runs, so one hung vendor cannot consume the shared worker fleet.
[w2] Deploys drain instead of killing: on SIGTERM the worker stops taking new jobs and lets the in-flight step commit its checkpoint, and the run continues on another instance.
keyPoints.quote: SIGTERM lets the current step checkpoint, then the run resumes on the next instance

keyPoints.text: [w1] The queue carries work, not truth: the run row exists in Postgres before the job is enqueued and the job is only a pointer, so a lost queue entry leaves a recoverable pending run instead of erased history.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — peak hour: the email vendor hangs for 6 minutes, two deploys land in the middle of the incident, and once the vendor is back on-call bulk-replays 10,000 dead-lettered runs. Walk the failure windows (what duplicates, what stalls, what pages late) and say what in your design, or in its gaps, decides each one.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Bulk replay is only as safe as the key it sends: a live replay clones the trigger into a fresh run id, nothing from the source run rehydrates under that id, and the vendorKey and dedupeWindow keys are built from run id + step id, so every replayed step goes out under a new key; only a content-derived naturalKey dedupes across runs.

[w3] A hung vendor saturates the shared fleet and healthy connectors queue behind it; in the drill, detection and the breaker worked but the alert fired minutes after customers felt it, so page on customer-visible symptoms and per-connector queue depth, not on the breaker trip.

[w3] A hard kill mid-step requeues the run, which resumes from its last checkpoint and re-executes the in-flight step; that repeat is harmless only where the vendor dedupes on the stable key, so the chat connector is exactly where a deploy can still double-post.

[w2] Replay discipline: sort the DLQ by error class and connector, confirm the root cause is fixed, dry-run a sample, then watch the failure rate; replaying into a vendor that is still broken only refills the DLQ.

[w2] Check the breaker's code against its contract: canRequest returns true whenever the state is not open, so after the cooldown every caller gets through during half-open rather than a single probe, and a recovering vendor receives the whole held backlog at once.
[w1] Rehydration requires storing outputs, so large vendor responses bloat the runs table; offload big outputs to object storage and keep only a reference in the row.
keyPoints.quote: Output must be persisted to rehydrate resumed steps

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your engine-operations choices against the alternatives the ADRs name. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Hand-rolled engine vs adopting Temporal or Restate now: full control and no new infrastructure, paid for by owning checkpoints, resume and replay yourself; having built the core once, adopting a framework later is an informed, sprint-sized move.
keyPoints.quote: a real team with this understanding could adopt Temporal in a sprint

keyPoints.text: [w3] Resuming from our own last write was rejected: it cannot tell what happened between the vendor's commit and ours, because the two systems commit at different instants, and only a key that travelled to the vendor bridges that gap.
keyPoints.quote: it cannot survive the gap between the two databases

keyPoints.text: [w3] Stuck-run alternatives: a hard timeout-and-fail kills legitimately slow runs, a blind timeout-and-retry pounds the same hung vendor and tightens the pileup, and hold-for-human needs 3am capacity nobody has; timing out to retriable-failed behind a breaker automates the common case.

[w2] Per-connector retry logic or retrying everything a few times: N inconsistent implementations the engine cannot bound, and re-sending deterministic failures spams bad requests and revoked tokens into vendor lockouts.
[w2] Exactly-once for every action is impossible when the vendor offers no idempotency; the honest design is an engine-side dedupe window plus an at-least-once warning shown to the builder.
keyPoints.quote: honest answer is `dedupeWindow` + an **at-least-once** warning surfaced in the builder

keyPoints.text: [w2] Replay is side-effect-gated: dry-run by default and live only on a deliberate choice, because a replay button that fires effects by default turns one misclick into thousands of real sends.
keyPoints.quote: dry-run by default, live is a deliberate click

keyPoints.text: [w1] Fail-fast vs continue-on-error: a run fails when a step exhausts its retries, because partial side effects across a half-run relay confuse users; real error paths belong in the DAG model.
